report:
Your answer is right: **no—ivermectin has not been shown to lower COVID-19 death risk** in trustworthy evidence. Early claims of large mortality benefits came from small, heterogeneous, sometimes high-risk-of-bias or withdrawn studies; once larger placebo-controlled/platform trials and guideline-grade syntheses were available, the apparent effect disappeared.

The best evidence is indirect for death in outpatients because deaths were rare, but it is still unfavorable: the TOGETHER randomized trial found ivermectin did **not** reduce COVID-19 progression leading to hospital admission or prolonged emergency-department observation (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869). ACTIV-6 likewise found no meaningful outpatient treatment benefit (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc2207995). Cochrane’s living review of randomized trials concluded the evidence did not support ivermectin for preventing or treating COVID-19, with certainty limited by study quality and imprecision rather than any clear survival advantage (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD015017_ivermectin-preventing-and-treating-covid-19; https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD015017.pub3/abstract).

Bottom line: if a true mortality effect existed, it is too small to have been detected consistently and is outweighed by the absence of benefit across higher-quality trials; major guidelines therefore recommend against routine use outside trials.
